q: What are the key ink properties calligraphers should understand?

What is ink shimmer?
What is the difference between shading ink and regular ink?
ink properties sheen shimmer shading chromatography multi-shading

a: Ink properties that matter most to calligraphers include flow (how readily the ink moves from nib to paper, affecting hairlines and smoothness), dry time (how long the ink remains wet, influencing smudging and the ability to work quickly), and water resistance (critical for projects that may be exposed to moisture or receive watercolor washes). Shading refers to the gradient from dark to light within a single stroke where ink pools at the bottom of a letter, with inks like Sailor Manyo and Diamine showcasing dramatic color variation known as chromatography. Sheen appears as a metallic film where ink dries thickest on coated paper (red sheen on dark green inks, gold sheen on dark blue inks), while shimmer inks contain suspended metallic particles that glitter when dry—both shader and shimmer properties require smooth, coated papers like Tomoe River or Rhodia to manifest fully.

a: Fountain pen friendly papers are defined by their ability to resist bleed-through (ink soaking through to the other side), feathering (ink spreading along paper fibers, creating fuzzy edges), and ghosting (shadow of writing visible from the reverse side). Popular paper brands include Tomoe River (67 gsm, known for exceptional sheen and shading display, though prone to ghosting due to its thinness), Rhodia (80-90 gsm, coated and smooth, reliable for all pen types, available in pads and notebooks), and Midori MD (high-quality, cream-colored paper with a toothy feel that enhances writing experience while remaining fountain pen friendly). For dip pen work, hot press watercolor paper (smooth, suitable for fine hairlines) and HP Premium 32 laser paper (affordable, bleed-resistant, good for practice) are popular, while cold press and rough watercolor papers suit broader brush techniques and wet media calligraphy.

a: Calligraphy guidelines are ruled sheets that indicate x-height (the height of lowercase letters), ascender and descender lines, and the slant angle, essential for maintaining consistent letter proportions and angle across a piece. Specialized practice pads like Nishiki Storyboards, Maruman graph pads, and Apica grid notebooks provide pre-printed guidelines for various scripts and nib widths, while Tsubame notebooks offer Fox River-style accounting paper with a smooth finish ideal for fountain pen practice. Slant boards (angled writing surfaces set at 20-45 degrees) improve wrist position and ink flow for dip pens, and light boxes allow calligraphers to place guided sheets beneath their working paper, providing visible guidelines without marking the final piece.

a: New nibs ship with a thin coating of manufacturing oils that prevent rust but also repel ink, requiring preparation by wiping with a potato (the natural starch cuts the oil), running the nib through a flame briefly, or cleaning with alcohol or toothpaste followed by thorough rinsing and drying. Between uses and color changes, dip nibs should be wiped clean with a soft cloth or rinsed in clean water, removing all ink residue to prevent clogging and corrosion, then dried completely and stored in a dry container with silica gel packets to prevent rust. Fountain pens require periodic flushing with lukewarm water (with a drop of dish soap for stubborn dried ink), disassembly for thorough cleaning of the nib and feed, and proper storage either upright or horizontally to maintain consistent ink flow.

a: Gilding is the application of gold or metallic leaf to calligraphy and illumination, creating luminous, reflective surfaces that have been prized in manuscript decoration since medieval times. The most common method is raised gilding, where a gesso compound (a mixture of fish glue, sugar, plaster, and bole clay) is built up in layers, allowed to dry partially, then coated with gold leaf that is pressed into the tacky surface and burnished with an agate burnisher to create a mirror-like finish. Shell gold (finely ground gold dust suspended in gum arabic) and modern metallic paints offer simpler alternatives for flat gilding applications, while glass gilding uses a transparent gesso technique that allows light to pass through the gold for a particularly luminous effect.
